Why rugged

What you are actually paying for

Rugged is a word that gets used loosely. Here is what it means on our devices, in terms you can check.

Sealed against dust and water

Every device is rated at least IP65: fully dust tight and protected against water jets from any direction. Most go further. An IP67 or IP68 rating means the housing survives immersion, not just a light shower, which is the difference between a tablet that survives a downpour and one that survives being dropped in a puddle. None is rated IP69K for high pressure jet washing, so wipe them down rather than hose them.

  • Gasket-sealed ports and a sealed speaker membrane
  • Removable batteries on the A6, A8, WH6 and W10, so a charged spare takes over mid shift
  • The A6, A10 and WH6 are rated from −20°C, so they start on a frosty morning

Built to be dropped

Three of the six devices, the A10, WH6 and W8, carry a MIL-STD-810H or 810G rating. The A6 is rated by its maker for 1.5 metre drops; the A8 and W10 list no drop standard. MIL-STD-810H is a published military test method, not a marketing phrase. The drop procedure means repeated falls from 1.22 metres (48 inches) onto plywood over concrete, across every face and corner, with the device still functioning afterwards.

In practice that comes from reinforced corners, a rubberised over-mould and a screen recessed behind a raised bezel, so the glass does not take the first hit when it lands face down.

Screens you can read outside, batteries that last the shift

A standard tablet runs about 400 nits, which washes out the moment you step outdoors. The A8 runs 1000 nits, so you are not cupping a hand over the screen to read a job number. The A10 is 350 nits, which suits drawings indoors and in the van more than bright sun. Each product page lists the maker's figure.

The A8 and A10 tablets carry 8,000mAh, against roughly 5,000mAh in a typical phone, and the A8's battery is removable. There is nothing clever about it; there is simply room inside a rugged body for a much larger cell. The A6 handheld is phone sized at 5,050mAh, but its battery is removable, so a charged spare takes over mid shift. Real run time depends on screen brightness and signal, so treat the capacity as a comparison, not a promise of hours.

FAQ

Questions worth asking before you buy

Six inch goes in a pocket and is right if you mostly scan barcodes, take photos, log jobs and stay in touch. Eight inch is the middle ground: big enough to fill in a form or follow a drawing, small enough for one hand and a van door pocket. Ten inch is for people who genuinely read drawings all day: blueprints, BIM viewers, full spreadsheets. If you are unsure, the 10.1 inch A10 is our pick for Android apps.

All three mean fully dust tight. The second digit is water: IP67 survives 1 metre of immersion for 30 minutes, IP68 goes deeper and longer, and IP69K adds resistance to high pressure, high temperature jets, which matters if your kit gets jet washed rather than just rained on. For most UK trades IP67 is genuinely enough; IP68 is the margin you want if the device lives outdoors. None of our devices is rated IP69K, so do not jet wash them.

Three of the six, the A10, WH6 and W8, are tested to MIL-STD-810H or 810G, which includes repeated 1.22 metre (48 inch) drops onto plywood over concrete. That is a real standard rather than marketing language. The A6 is rated by its maker for 1.5 metre drops, and the A8 and W10 list no drop standard, so treat those with more care if they live on a scaffold. It does not make a device indestructible. It means the housing, corners and screen are engineered for the kind of drop that kills a consumer tablet.

Android if you are using apps: job management, forms, photos, maps, cloud tools. That covers most trades and it is cheaper. Windows only if you need actual desktop software that has no mobile version: diagnostic tools, legacy databases, GIS, CAD viewers or network drives. Windows devices cost £200 to £350 more than the Android model of the same size, so do not buy one unless a specific piece of software forces your hand.
